title: Doubled and Absent Values in a Grid
statement:
An n × n grid was meant to hold every number from 1 to n² exactly once. One mistake crept in: one number was written twice, and because of that a different number is missing.

Return [doubled, missing], in that order.

examples.why: The values 1 to 4 should appear once each. 4 shows up twice and 3 never appears.
The doubled value comes first in the answer, even though it is the larger number here.
The missing value can be n² itself. A scan that only looks for gaps between values it has seen would miss it.

constraints: Exactly one value appears twice and exactly one value in 1..n² is absent
hints: You know exactly which values should be present. What do you need to remember about each one while you read the grid?
Keep a count for every value from 1 to n². After one pass, the value counted twice is the doubled one and the value counted zero times is the missing one.
Without extra memory: the grid's sum differs from 1 + 2 + … + n² by (doubled − missing). The sum of squares gives (doubled² − missing²). Divide the second by the first to get (doubled + missing).

explain.intuition:
The grid is a checklist of the values 1..n². Read every cell and tick off its value in a counts array. One value ends up ticked twice and one value is never ticked. That is the whole problem: a single pass plus a scan of the counts.

There is also an arithmetic way. Compare the actual sum with the expected sum N(N+1)/2: the difference is d = doubled − missing. Do the same with squares and you get doubled² − missing² = d · (doubled + missing). Two equations, two unknowns. It uses O(1) memory, but the counting version is easier to get right in an interview.
steps: Let N = n² and make a counts array of size N + 1, all zero.
Walk v from 1 to N: if counts[v] === 2, that is the doubled value; if counts[v] === 0, that is the missing one.
pitfalls: Returning the pair in the wrong order. The doubled value comes first.
Scanning the counts only up to the largest value seen. The missing value can be n² itself.
Looking for the missing value as a gap between neighbours after sorting. That misses 1 and n² when they are the absent ones.

solutions.title: Count every value
solutions.idea: Tally each value in an array indexed by value, then read off the one seen twice and the one never seen.

solutions.title: Sum and sum of squares
solutions.idea: The sum is off by doubled − missing; the sum of squares is off by doubled² − missing². Dividing gives doubled + missing, and two linear equations finish it.
solutions.py:
class Solution:
    def doubledAndAbsent(self, grid: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
        N = len(grid) * len(grid)
        s = sum(v for row in grid for v in row)
        sq = sum(v * v for row in grid for v in row)
        diff = s - N * (N + 1) // 2                      # doubled - missing
        sq_diff = sq - N * (N + 1) * (2 * N + 1) // 6    # doubled^2 - missing^2
        total = sq_diff // diff                          # doubled + missing
        return [(total + diff) // 2, (total - diff) // 2]

followups: The values arrive as a stream too large to store. Which of the two solutions still works?
Two values are doubled and two are missing. Is sum plus sum of squares still enough?
